power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("File Name" = c("meta_2_script.R", "meta_2_script.R" ), "% Comments" = c("31%", "31%"), "Missing Files" = c(0L, 0L ), "Absolute Paths" = c(0L, 0L), "Code Between Libraries" = c(1L, 1L)), row.names = 1:2, class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ```
#### Code Comments
Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.
#### Missing Files
All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.
#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Libraries / Imports
Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.
#### Packages / Dependencies
The code files load 4 distinct packages/libraries: ggpubr, metafor, RoBMA, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).
#### Reproducible Environment

No `renv.lock` file, `sessionInfo()`/`session_info()` record, or `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an `renv.lock` (via the `renv` package), a `sessionInfo()` text dump, or a `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin alongside the code.
#### Parsable code
All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

info.title: Can GenAI Boost Writing Scores? Another Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis (RoBMA) of Writing Ability

text.text: A new meta-analysis (Teng, 2026) has shown that genAI has a strong impact on writing with similar effects as another recent meta-analysis (Dong, 2026).
text.formatted: A new meta-analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Teng, 2026)</ref> has shown that genAI has a strong impact on writing with similar effects as another recent meta-analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Dong, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The current analysis instead shows a much weaker effect after correcting for entry errors and heterogeneity.
M.F. Teng, Effectiveness of GenAI in enhancing writing performance: A meta-analysis.
Asian-Pacific Journal of Second and Foreign Language Education, 11(1), 70 (2026), doi: https://doi.org/10.1186/s40862-026-00444-2
text.formatted: Asian-Pacific Journal of Second and Foreign Language Education, 11(1), 70 (2026), doi: <ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.1186/s40862-026-00444-2">https://doi.org/10.1186/s40862-026- 00444-2</ref>

text.text: Teng [1] reported that genAI's impact on writing is substantial (Hedge's g = 0.80[0.37, 1.22]), which mirrors another meta-analysis on writing (Hedge's g = .76[.18, 1.35]) [2].
text.formatted: Teng <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> reported that genAI's impact on writing is substantial (Hedge's g = 0.80[0.37, 1.22]), which mirrors another meta-analysis on writing (Hedge's g = .76[.18, 1.35]) <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Teng's analysis similarly included extreme heterogeneity and a small study sample.
Consequently, Teng provided faithful attempts at robustness checks (e.g.
PET-PEESE).
Unfortunately, these methods are often not robust effective [3].
text.formatted: Unfortunately, these methods are often not robust effective <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: The current analysis uses a robust version of meta-analysis, RoBMA [4], which accounts for these issues.
text.formatted: The current analysis uses a robust version of meta-analysis, RoBMA <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>, which accounts for these issues.

text.text: It follows a similar attempt to "robustify" Dong's study [5].
text.formatted: It follows a similar attempt to "robustify" Dong's study <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: This analysis used the RoBMA meta-analysis package [4] with R Version 4.6.0.
text.formatted: This analysis used the RoBMA meta-analysis package <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> with R Version 4.6.0.

text.text: Most default priors were used for the model.
They assume that bias is present and consequently pull parameters closer to zero.
An explicit prior was used for the main parameter µ, the average effect of the intervention.
This parameter estimated the standardized mean difference of genAI vs nonAI on writing with Hedge's g [3].
text.formatted: This parameter estimated the standardized mean difference of genAI vs nonAI on writing with Hedge's g <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: The prior was set to: µ ∼ Normal(.40, 1) This prior was based on the average effect of educational interventions [6].
text.formatted: The prior was set to: µ ∼ Normal(.40, 1) This prior was based on the average effect of educational interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: The analysis used 10,000 samples and 5 chains to increase effective sample size (ESS).
Terminology in this paper can be found in Harrer et al. (2021) [3].
text.formatted: Terminology in this paper can be found in Harrer et al. (2021) <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: I was not able to reproduce the data obtained in the original meta-analysis.
First, one article incorrectly coded an effect as positive [7].
text.formatted: First, one article incorrectly coded an effect as positive <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Second, another article had many post-test outcomes but I was not able to reproduce the effect used in the final-meta analysis.
Consequently, I used Teng's criteria of an "overall writing" measure by including the standardized effect size of "task achievement" in the original study [8].
text.formatted: Consequently, I used Teng's criteria of an "overall writing" measure by including the standardized effect size of "task achievement" in the original study <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: The RoBMA model showed that the estimated effect (in Figure 1) was much lower than the original effect and indistinguishable from statistical noise (g = .319[-.026, .956], BF = 1.681).
text.formatted: The RoBMA model showed that the estimated effect (in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>) was much lower than the original effect and indistinguishable from statistical noise (g = .319[-.026, .956], BF = 1.681).

text.text: Unlike Dong's study, this analysis had no obvious outliers or small-study bias, but shared extreme heterogeneity (nearly 100%, BF > 49,999).
text.formatted: Unlike Dong's study, this analysis had no obvious outliers or small-study bias, but shared extreme heterogeneity (nearly 100%, BF > 49,999).

text.text: Some minor selection bias may have been present, (see z-curve plot in Figure 1), but this did not seem to shape the result as much as heterogeneity.
text.formatted: Some minor selection bias may have been present, (see z-curve plot in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), but this did not seem to shape the result as much as heterogeneity.

text.text: This re-analysis doesn't support the original claim of strong effects after correcting for entry errors and heterogeneity.
Reproducibility The original data and Python script from the target article was not available online.

While I was able to reproduce most of the data by-hand by searching through the cited articles, one study was miscoded as a positive effect while another seemed to not match any of the post-test outcomes in the final meta-analysis.
As such, I was not able to reproduce what the original author intended with the analysis.
